- deep-research: Deep research harness — fan-out web searches, fetch sources, adversarially verify claims, synthesize a cited report. - When the user wants a deep, multi-source, fact-checked research report on any topic. BEFORE invoking, check if the question is specific enough to research directly — if underspecified (e.g., "what car to buy" without budget/use-case/region), ask 2-3 clarifying questions to narrow scope. Then pass the refined question as args, weaving the answers in.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- verify: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by exercising it end-to-end and observing behavior — drive the affected flow, not just tests or typecheck. Run before committing nontrivial changes; bootstraps this repo's project verify skill if none exists yet. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.
- code-review: Review the current diff for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings). Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo, defaults to 10m) - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- review: Review a GitHub pull request; for your working diff use /code-review
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

input.equal_range_semantics:
tsl::hopscotch_map is a UNIQUE-key (std::unordered_map-like) container, so equal_range degenerates to a "0-or-1 element" range, exactly like std::unordered_map::equal_range.

Contract, expressed in terms of find()/end():
  auto it = find(key);
  if (it == end()) return {end(), end()};   // key ABSENT -> empty range
  else             return {it, std::next(it)}; // key PRESENT -> half-open range covering exactly that one element

- Key PRESENT: range.first points at the single element whose key compares equal; range.second is the immediate successor position in iteration order (which is end() when the found element happens to be last in iteration order). Therefore std::distance(range.first, range.second) == 1 and the counting loop `for (it = first; it != second; ++it) num_in_range++` executes its body exactly once -> yields 1.
- Key ABSENT: range.first == range.second (both end(), or more generally two equal iterators), the loop condition `it != second` is false on entry -> yields 0.
- Consequence: num_in_range is always identical to map.count(key), i.e. it is a boolean-valued 0/1 presence test. Multiplicity can never exceed 1 because insert() on a duplicate key is a no-op that returns {existing_iterator, false}. So the "range" concept from multimaps (where equal_range can span N>1 equal keys) never produces N>1 here. This is the whole point of the test: it pins equal_range to unique-key semantics.
- Bucket-order caveat that does NOT affect the count: hopscotch hashing means iteration order is unspecified/implementation-defined, so WHICH element range.second names varies with count and hash layout, but the DISTANCE is invariantly 1. A faithful port must not try to reproduce C++ iteration order; it only has to reproduce distance == 1 (present) / 0 (absent).
input.expected_output_rule:
Keys inserted are exactly {0, 1, ..., count-1} (the loop `for (i=0; i<count; i++)` runs max(count,0) times). The queried key is `count / 2` using C++ INTEGER division, which truncates toward ZERO (so -1/2 == 0, -3/2 == -1, -1000000/2 == -500000).

CLOSED FORM:
    printed = (count >= 1) ? 1 : 0
equivalently `if count > 0 { 1 } else { 0 }`  -- i.e. `usize::from(count > 0)`.

Proof of the two branches:
- count <= 0 (includes all negatives and 0): the insert loop body never executes, so the map is EMPTY. Any query key is absent -> equal_range gives an empty range -> prints 0. (Note the queried key is still computed, e.g. count=-3 queries -1, count=-1 queries 0, count=0 queries 0, but an empty map contains nothing, so the value of the key is irrelevant.)
- count >= 1: we need 0 <= count/2 <= count-1 so that count/2 is one of the inserted keys.
    * Lower bound: count >= 1 > 0 so floor(count/2) >= 0.
    * Upper bound: floor(count/2) <= count-1 holds for every count >= 1 (count=1: 0 <= 0; count=2: 1 <= 1; and for count >= 2 the gap count-1-floor(count/2) = ceil(count/2)-1 >= 0 and grows).
  So the key is ALWAYS present, and by unique-key semantics the range has exactly one element -> prints 1.

Per-case table requested:
- count < 0            -> 0   (empty map; key = trunc-toward-zero count/2, irrelevant)
- count == 0           -> 0   (empty map, key 0 absent)
- count == 1           -> 1   (keys {0}, key 1/2 == 0, present -- the tight boundary case)
- count == 2           -> 1   (keys {0,1}, key 2/2 == 1, present -- the other tight boundary: key equals the LAST inserted key, so range.second may be end())
- odd count >= 1       -> 1   (key = (count-1)/2, strictly interior for count >= 3)
- even count >= 2      -> 1   (key = count/2, interior for count >= 4)
- large count (up to 9,999,999 verified; holds for all count up to INT_MAX) -> 1
- default, no args (count = 15) -> 1

PARITY AND MAGNITUDE ARE IRRELEVANT. The only discriminator is emptiness of the map, i.e. sign/zero-ness of count. There is no count >= 1 that prints anything other than 1, and no count <= 0 that prints anything other than 0. A correct Rust port therefore prints exactly two possible values, 0 and 1.

Argument-parsing behavior the port must also match (observed):
- No args, or argv[1] != "--a" (e.g. `--b 7`): count stays 15 -> prints 1, exit 0.
- `--a <n>`: count = stoi(n).
- `--a` with NO argv[2]: C++ constructs std::string from a NULL pointer -> throws std::logic_error "basic_string::_S_construct null not valid" -> abort, exit 134, nothing printed on stdout. (Rust: this is a panic/abort path, not a 0.)
- `--a abc` (no leading digits): std::stoi throws std::invalid_argument -> abort, exit 134.
- `--a 9xyz`: std::stoi parses the leading digits and IGNORES the trailing junk -> count = 9 -> prints 1, exit 0. A naive Rust `str::parse::<i32>()` would FAIL here, so the port needs stoi-style prefix parsing to be faithful.
api_surface_needed: DEFAULT CONSTRUCTION -- C++: tsl::hopscotch_map<int,int> map;  =>  Rust: `impl<K: Hash + Eq, V> HopscotchMap<K, V> { pub fn new() -> Self }` plus `impl<K: Hash + Eq, V> Default for HopscotchMap<K, V> { fn default() -> Self }`. Must start empty with len()==0 and no heap allocation required to be observable. REQUIRED by the test.

INSERT OF A PAIR -- C++: std::pair<iterator,bool> insert(std::pair<K,V>&& value)  =>  Rust: `pub fn insert_pair(&mut self, value: (K, V)) -> (Cursor, bool)`. The C++ call site uses brace-init `map.insert({i, i * 12})`, i.e. it passes a std::pair, NOT two separate args -- a faithful port takes a single `(K, V)` tuple. The bool is `true` if a NEW element was inserted, `false` if an element with an equal key already existed (in which case the map is UNCHANGED -- the old value is kept, it is NOT overwritten; this is what guarantees unique keys and hence range size <= 1). The Cursor points at the new-or-existing element. REQUIRED by the test (return value is discarded by this test, but the no-overwrite-on-duplicate semantics must exist for a faithful library translation, and the pair-taking overload is the exact one exercised).

IDIOMATIC RUST COMPANION FOR INSERT -- `pub fn insert(&mut self, key: K, value: V) -> Option<V>` (std::collections::HashMap style, returns the displaced value). NOT exercised by the test and NOT equivalent to C++ insert (Rust HashMap::insert OVERWRITES; C++ insert does not). If the port exposes this name it must be documented as different from the C++ `insert`; the C++-faithful one should be `insert_pair` / `try_insert`. Optional, but if present it must not be what the ported test calls.

EQUAL_RANGE -- C++: std::pair<iterator,iterator> equal_range(const Key& key); (and a const overload returning std::pair<const_iterator,const_iterator>)  =>  Rust: `pub fn equal_range(&self, key: &K) -> (Cursor, Cursor)`. Returns (find(key), successor-of-find(key)) when present, and (end(), end()) when absent. Must be callable on a shared borrow. REQUIRED by the test. A second `pub fn equal_range_mut(&mut self, key: &K) -> (CursorMut, CursorMut)` mirrors the non-const C++ overload and MUST exist for a faithful library translation even though the test only needs the const form.

EQUAL_RANGE AS AN ITERATOR (the pragmatic Rust shape) -- `pub fn equal_range_iter(&self, key: &K) -> EqualRange<'_, K, V>` where `impl<'a, K, V> Iterator for EqualRange<'a, K, V> { type Item = (&'a K, &'a V); }`. This lets the ported counting loop be written as `map.equal_range_iter(&key).count()`, which is the idiomatic rendering of the C++ `for (it = range.first; it != range.second; ++it) num_in_range++`. Recommended; a `(Cursor, Cursor)` pair alone cannot be walked in safe Rust without also exposing the two items below.

ITERATOR/CURSOR TYPE -- C++ uses a forward iterator supporting `++it` (pre-increment) and `it != other`  =>  Rust needs a position type: `#[derive(Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)] pub struct Cursor(usize);` (an index into the internal bucket array, with a sentinel value meaning end()). REQUIRED so that `(Cursor, Cursor)` from equal_range is meaningful.

ITERATOR INCREMENT -- C++: iterator& operator++()  =>  Rust: `pub fn advance(&mut self, map: &HopscotchMap<K, V>)` or, cleanly, fold the increment into the `Iterator::next` impl of `EqualRange`/`Iter`. Semantics: move to the next OCCUPIED bucket in internal order, skipping empty buckets; landing past the last occupied bucket yields end(). REQUIRED by the test's loop (the `++it` step).

ITERATOR INEQUALITY / EQUALITY -- C++: bool operator!=(const iterator&, const iterator&) (and operator==)  =>  Rust: `impl PartialEq for Cursor` / `#[derive(PartialEq, Eq)]`, so `first != second` works. Two cursors are equal iff they denote the same slot (or both are end()). REQUIRED by the test's loop condition.

ITERATOR DEREFERENCE -- C++: std::pair<const K, V>& operator*() and operator->  =>  Rust: `pub fn get(&self, cur: Cursor) -> Option<(&K, &V)>` or `Iterator::Item = (&'a K, &'a V)`. NOT exercised by this test (the loop only counts, never dereferences), but MUST exist for a faithful library translation -- an iterator you cannot dereference is not an iterator.

FIND -- C++: iterator find(const Key&); const_iterator find(const Key&) const  =>  Rust: `pub fn find(&self, key: &K) -> Cursor` and the idiomatic `pub fn get(&self, key: &K) -> Option<&V>`. Not named at the call site, but equal_range is DEFINED in terms of it, so it must exist internally; expose it for a faithful translation.

END SENTINEL -- C++: iterator end(); const_iterator end() const  =>  Rust: `pub fn end(&self) -> Cursor` (or a `Cursor::END` constant). Required to express the absent-key result of equal_range and to terminate iteration. Must exist for a faithful translation; the test reaches it implicitly whenever the found element is last in iteration order.

COUNT / CONTAINS -- C++: size_type count(const Key&) const; bool contains(const Key&) const  =>  Rust: `pub fn count(&self, key: &K) -> usize` (returns only 0 or 1) and `pub fn contains_key(&self, key: &K) -> bool`. Not called by the test, but `count()` is numerically IDENTICAL to what this test computes, so it is the natural cross-check for the port's equal_range implementation. Should exist for a faithful translation.

SIZE / EMPTINESS -- C++: size_type size() const; bool empty() const  =>  Rust: `pub fn len(&self) -> usize` and `pub fn is_empty(&self) -> bool`. Not called by the test, but needed for a faithful translation and for the count <= 0 empty-map branch to be assertable.

WHOLE-MAP ITERATION -- C++: begin()/end() yielding forward iterators  =>  Rust: `pub fn iter(&self) -> Iter<'_, K, V>` with `impl Iterator for Iter`, plus `impl<'a, K, V> IntoIterator for &'a HopscotchMap<K, V>`. Not exercised by the test, but the equal_range cursor pair is only coherent if a global iteration order exists, so the machinery must be there for a faithful translation.

TRAIT BOUNDS -- C++ template params <Key, T, Hash = std::hash<Key>, KeyEqual = std::equal_to<Key>>  =>  Rust: `K: Hash + Eq`, with the default hasher supplied by std (`std::collections::hash_map::RandomState` or a hand-rolled std-only hasher, since ZERO external crates are allowed). The test instantiates K = i32, V = i32 (i32 to match C++ `int` overflow-wrap semantics for `i * 12`; note i*12 is only stored, never read, so it cannot affect output -- but use i32/wrapping_mul to stay faithful for large counts).

GROWTH / REHASH INTERNALS -- C++ hopscotch_map silently rehashes as load factor is exceeded (exercised implicitly by the test at counts up to ~10 million)  =>  Rust: private `fn rehash(&mut self, new_capacity: usize)`. Not public API the test names, but the port MUST handle growth correctly or large-count runs will break; the empirical spread (4095/4096/4097, 65535/65536/65537, 1e6, 1e7) exists precisely to catch a port whose resize logic loses or duplicates keys, which would turn the printed 1 into 0 or 2.
